summary:
Mission Architect is a browser game built on Gmat-Web, our web port of NASA's open-source General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). Players choose a campaign. On the Moon they search for water ice at the south pole, based on LCROSS and VIPER. On Mars they hunt rocks and minerals, based on Curiosity and Perseverance. Each mission runs from start to finish: an Atlas V launch, a transfer trajectory that GMAT computes live, landing-site selection on a 3D globe with real elevation data, a landing cinematic, and rover work with ChemCam-style laser scans, drilling to real depths, sample tubes, dust storms, power limits and event cards.

Our project addresses the challenge by turning a professional flight-dynamics tool into an interactive experience. Every trajectory, landing site and instrument comes from real NASA missions and datasets, so players face the same trade-offs mission engineers do. This matters because mission design usually sits behind expert software. Mission Architect makes it easy for students and the public to get into, without giving up scientific accuracy.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

1. Mission choice. The player picks the Moon or Mars, and each has its own story, objectives and science goal. On the Moon the goal is to find water ice in permanently shadowed regions. On Mars it is to find and analyze rocks and minerals that could preserve signs of past habitability.

2. Launch and transfer. A 3D Atlas V launch cinematic climbs through the layers of the atmosphere. Then the spacecraft follows the curved transfer trajectory that GMAT computes live, which shows that spacecraft do not fly in a straight line.

3.Site selection and mapping. The player chooses from real landing sites (for example Jezero, Gale, Gusev, Elysium and Hellas on Mars) on an interactive 3D globe. Each site's terrain comes from real elevation data, such as the USGS LRO LOLA + SELENE/Kaguya lunar DEM.

4.Entry, descent and landing. The player makes step-by-step decisions during descent (parachute, sky crane), followed by a rover deployment cinematic.

5. Surface operations. The player drives a Curiosity-based rover with procedural suspension over real terrain. On Mars, the laser scanner (ChemCam-style) identifies rock types, and the drill (5 cm, the depth Curiosity actually used) works by holding the key with a progress bar and its own close-up camera. On the Moon, a VIPER-style vertical drill works in stages with intermediate readings, tracks bit temperature and shows a live gas spectrum. Navigation cameras show a hazard grid and suggest a safe path.

6.Resource and risk management. Battery and solar charging are limited, dust builds up on the panels, and there is day/night and light versus shadow. Mars has sandstorms that you shelter from behind hills, plus cold. Only 3 sample tubes are available, and instrument hours in the Earth lab are limited. A stress-based event-card deck brings in real mission problems such as solar conjunction, global dust storms, a swollen atmosphere and late commands.

7.Results. Sealed samples are analyzed in an Earth lab, which ends in a press announcement and an epilogue that reflects how well the mission went.

What benefits does it have?

  • The trade-offs become concrete. Students feel the tension between science return, power, time, risk and communications instead of just reading about it.
  • It is scientifically grounded. The trajectories come from GMAT. The terrain, planet sizes (NASA mean radii), landing sites, rock cases (for example Cheyava Falls and John Klein), instruments and drill depths all come from real missions.
  • It covers the whole mission lifecycle. Launch, transfer, landing site, EDL, operations, sample analysis and results are all in one experience.
  • Students can try again. Two different campaigns and changing events mean they can replay, compare strategies and learn from failures.
  • It is accessible. It runs in a web browser with no installation

What is the intended impact?

We want students who rarely get to touch real mission design to understand how a mission is designed and why engineers make the choices they do. By putting a real NASA tool and real data behind a game, we want to spark interest in aerospace engineering and planetary science, especially among students without access to professional software or labs. In the long term, Mission Architect could become a classroom and outreach tool where new missions are added as GMAT scripts.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Simulation core: NASA GMAT
  • Backend: Python with FastAPI
  • Frontend: TypeScript with React (TSX), Three.js for real-time 3D, and Vite
  • 3D assets: Blender used to optimize, rig and export the Curiosity/MSL model as GLB
  • Data: USGS LRO LOLA + SELENE/Kaguya merged lunar DEM, Mars elevation data and textures, NASA planetary mean radii, and a Natural Earth II texture for Earth
  • DevOps: Docker, plus Git/GitHub with feature branches for each mechanic
  • AI-assisted development: Claude Code (multi-agent workflow with a dedicated QA agent) and Claude in Chrome for automated in-browser testing and capturing trailer footage
  • Design: the custom "Flight Data File" UI system with IBM Plex typography
  • Hardware: the team's Windows and Linux laptops with dedicated GPUs (NVIDIA) for WebGL rendering

How is our project creative?

  • It turns a professional NASA trajectory tool into the engine of a game, so the physics are real, not scripted.
  • It mixes flight simulation with tabletop game design, taking ideas from D&D, Baldur's Gate and Nemesis: a stress-based event deck, engineering rolls, timers and secret objectives.
  • Each world plays the way its real mission did. The Moon is about prospecting for ice in darkness. Mars is about rock science under dust storms.
  • It reuses one rover model in two roles: the Curiosity rig becomes a VIPER-style lunar prospector, with the arm turned into a vertical drill tower.
  • It adds cinematic touches: drill close-ups with an x-ray view of the rock, scanning close-ups, camera shake and dust on the lens during storms, and a real-scale solar-system title screen.
  • It has its own visual identity inspired by real mission documents, avoiding generic sci-fi or "AI-looking" interfaces.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Scientific accuracy: real missions (LCROSS, VIPER, Curiosity, Perseverance), real datasets, real drill depths, instruments and planet sizes. Each mission's mechanics follow what really happened (water on the Moon, rocks on Mars).
  • The challenge's trade-offs: mission objectives, instruments, launch vehicle, power, communications and orbital constraints, all expressed as decisions with consequences.
  • Playability and learning curve: clear objectives, readable UI, step-by-step decision panels, hints (clue maps, safe-path suggestions) and a rover reset so players don't get stuck.
  • Performance: a low-poly rover, a shared texture cache, pre-warmed viewers and anti-tiling techniques so the game runs smoothly in a browser.
  • Accessibility and deployment: web-based, dockerized and in English.
  • Teamwork and maintainability: a feature branch for each mechanic, careful merges, documentation, a QA agent and logged prompts for transparency about how AI was used.
